summary: Year 3 learners add and subtract within 1000 by extending the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary: ten tens make a hundred, and a hundred can be broken back into ten tens. Taught concretely then pictorially then in writing for the SAME calculation, so 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. Across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137) is the hardest, most error-prone case and deserves deliberate attention.
misconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction across any column (e.g. ones done as larger-minus-smaller)
Failing to compose a hundred: ten or more tens left in the tens place (170+80 recorded with 15 in the tens column)
Borrow-across-zero errors: decomposing when the adjacent column is 0 (402−137) done incorrectly
Treating each column independently with no exchange, so carried/borrowed units vanish

activities.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
steps: Lay out 256 and 167 with base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) on a H-T-O mat.
Combine the ones: 6+7=13. Exchange ten ones for one ten and move that ten into the tens column (leave 3 ones).
Combine the tens: 5+6+1(carried)=12 tens. Exchange ten tens for one hundred and move it into the hundreds column (leave 2 tens).
Combine the hundreds: 2+1+1(carried)=4. Read the result: 423.
Record the matching written steps beside the blocks — first in an expanded layout, then in compact columns — so each written mark names a physical exchange.
activities.insight: Carrying across two columns is the same exchange move repeated at a second boundary: ten ones become one ten, and ten tens become one hundred.

activities.title: Cascade across a zero: 402 − 137
steps: Build 402 with blocks on the mat (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones).
Try to subtract the ones (2−7): there aren't enough, and there are no tens to borrow — notice the empty tens column.
Break one hundred into ten tens (now 3 hundreds, 10 tens, 2 ones).
Break one of those tens into ten ones (now 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones). This is 402 written as 300+90+12.
Narrate each exchange aloud before recording it, so the two-step cascade is spoken and written in order.
activities.insight: When a column is empty you cannot borrow directly; you must first decompose the next higher unit to fill it, then decompose again — a cascade, not a one-step borrow.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: reveal each exchange step
steps: Study a worked addition and a worked across-zero subtraction with each exchange step hidden until requested.
Before revealing, predict what happens to a pile of ten tens, or where a borrowed ten in an empty column comes from.
Reveal the step (e.g. the tens pile becoming one hundred and some tens; the zero column being fed from a decomposed hundred) and compare it with your prediction.
Explain in your own words why the unit moved one column over.
activities.insight: Each written exchange step corresponds to a specific regrouping of units; a step-by-step reference makes the structure of the double regroup visible.

activities.title: Consolidation practice with across-zero and compose-a-hundred checks
steps: Work a mixed set of three-digit additions and subtractions, including several across-a-zero subtractions.
For 170+80, choose the correct result and explain why '15 tens' (a two-digit entry in the tens column) is wrong — ten of those tens must become a hundred (250).
Fill in the decomposition of 402 as 300+90+12 and use it to complete 402−137.
Check each answer by estimating and, where possible, by the inverse operation.
activities.insight: Fluent recording still depends on composing a hundred and decomposing across a zero; checking with estimation and inverse catches slips.

checkQuestion: Give the child base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) and paper and set two calculations to work with the apparatus and record: 256 + 167, then 402 − 137. Watch what happens at each column, and especially at the zero in 402.
checkAnswer: 423 and 265. For 256+167: ones 6+7=13 (compose a ten), tens 5+6+1=12 (compose a hundred), hundreds 2+1+1=4 → 423. For 402−137: no tens to give ones, so decompose a hundred into ten tens then a ten into ten ones (402 as 300+90+12), 12−7=5, 90−30=60, 300−100=200 → 265.
